title: Town of Pullman Records, 1876-1919.
creator: Pullman Company. Manufacturing Dept.$$QPullman Company. Manufacturing Dept.
desc: Journals, ledgers, plats, an atlas, land surveys, and other miscellaneous records regarding the town of Pullman, 1876-1919. Financial records include a journal of town construction accounts (including payrolls), 1882-1886, and ledgers recording personal loans to town residents, 1897-1900, and mortgage loans, 1909-1919, for town real estate (listing purchaser's names, date, lot and block numbers, and principal and interest payments).  Property records include Lake Calumet surveys, field notes, maps, and diagrams, 1879-1899, plats of town property showing structures, 1907, and an atlas of town and other corporate properties, 1904. There is also an 1886 statement of tenement capacities in Pullman, an essay describing the town in 1890, and an Arcade Theatre program, 1883.

title: French notarial registers
desc: French notarial registers or "actes notoriés", containing summaries of documents executed by various notaries in France, during the years 1410-1749. Three registers (vols. 4,11, nd 13) were compiled by notaries in the Languédoc town of Saint-Pons, although the fact that the registers were purchased as a lot, as well as similarities in their size and binding style, suggest that all fifteen vols. may have originated in Saint-Pons.  Although the registers spanned almost 350 years, the notaries who compiled them remained very consistent in the types of transactions they documented, and the formulaic language they used. Types of documents summarized include wills ("testament"), marriage certificates ("mariage entre..."), land sales ("achat"), leases of land ("bail") and livestock ("cheptel"), cancellations of debt ("quittance"), promissory notes ("obligation de payer"), and division of a decedant's estate among heirs ("partage").  Notaries whose signatures appear throughout include Guillaume Peytraud [?] Girard Bonnaud, Bartholomé Martinel, Pierre Mathieu, Louis Mathieu, Antoine Mathieu, Anthoine Champsaur, Jacob de St. Roman, and Jean Richaud.

title: Relacion politica y civil del virreynato de Lima que hizo el S[en]or Amad con respecto al t[iem]po de su gobierno
creator: Peru. Viceroy (1761-1776 : Amat)$$QPeru. Viceroy (1761-1776 : Amat)
desc: Summaries and excerpts from Relación de gobierno by Manuel Amat y Junient, 31st viceroy of Peru from 1761 to 1776. In his Relación, Amat describes for his successor the status of the viceroyalty, his major accomplishments while in office, important events of his administration, and problems that still need to be addressed.  This ms., undated and compiled by an unknown copyist, includes some excerpts and charts from the lengthy original document; most other chapters have been drastically shortened or paraphrased.  The report deals with ecclesiastical, political, civil, and financial matters of the viceroyalty, and covers such topics as the inquisition, universities, mines, taxes and customs, government tobacco monopoly, pensions, hostilities with the Indians, and revenues and balances of the subtreasuries of the kingdom.  Only a few of the tables found in the original document are included here, providing details on official salaries, population statistics, number of priests by district, and total tax revenues.

title: Discorso, ovvero breve ristretto sopra le regole del canto fermo ad uso di me [monogram]  1781-1782.
creator: FBDC.$$QFBDC.
desc: Ms. from Italy, dated 1781, perhaps compiled by a choir master, or a student in an ecclesiastical school, containing basic notes for a course in singing Gregorian chants, with a separate section of calligraphic alphabets. The first section begins with the diagram of a musical hand divided into nineteen parts, the numbered arrangement of which corresponds to the chords of Gregorian chant. The accompanying explanatory notes in Italian discuss rhythm, notes, chords, key, and intonation, and include numerous musical examples of liturgical chants, indicating the type of chant--psalms, canticles, hymns, benedictions--and the church-year service in which they were sung. The second section contains twelve calligraphic alphabets, some created by the calligrapher, and others copied from contemporary writing manuals. One of the examples, an elaborate Gothic alphabet, contains three versions of each letter, arranged in horizontal rows of three compartments, each version shaped differently and embellished with different motifs, such as stars, snakes, grotesque faces, organ pipes, and the ecclesiastical monogram IHS. The letters are drawn in black ink against cross-hatched backgrounds in brown, orange, and red and black inks. In another example, an alphabet of 24 roman capitals (omitting "I" and "W"), arranged in six rows of four squares, have architectural backgrounds depicting tiny finely-drawn buildings, arches, piazzas, aqueducts, clock towers, bell towers, and domes. title: [Calendar].
creator: Newberry Library. Manuscript. Case MS 127.$$QNewberry Library.
desc: Six folded parchment sheets comprising a 15th century vade macum almanac created for use in England. Sheets were folded horizontally then vertically and attached by a tab to a belt. Leaves contain a calendar for one of the twelve months with names of important saints' days celebrated universally by the Catholic Church, as well as those of a more local interest. Includes 29 columns in brown and red containing Golden Numbers, hours of midnight and midday, the position and altitude of the sun at midday, the hours at which the planets are visible, and the Dominical Letters. To the right are similar columns containing the time in hours and minutes when the stars [constellations?] are in certain positions. Includes additional astronomical tables about the movement of the planets, eclipses of the sun, and the signs of the zodiac with space left for an unexecuted illustration of a Zodiac man. The last leaf had text describing bloodletting and locations of veins with space left for an unexecuted illustration of a Vein man.

creator: Porée, Charles, 1675-1741. Ecole des pères.$$QPorée, Charles | Porée, Charles, 1675-1741. Trossuli, ou les petits maistres.$$QPorée, Charles | Ingoult, Nicolas-Louis, S.J. Hypoptophilus sive suspicax.$$QIngoult, Nicolas-Louis | Collège Louis-le-Grand (Paris, France)$$QCollège Louis-le-Grand (Paris, France)
desc: Unsigned ms. miscellany of 18th-century plays, debates, speeches, poems, and mathematical lessons, probably copied for use in academies, boarding schools, and charitable institutions sometime between 1716 and 1735. Father Charles Porée's plays, L'ecole des pères (1717), and Trossuli, or, Les petits maitres (1717) are included, as are 3 plays by his fellow Jesuit Nicolas-Louis Ingoult: Le bel esprit (1716); Pyrrhus (1716); and Hypoptophilus sive suspicax (1716).  Also included are texts of 3 debates, 2 in French and 1 in Latin, presented by students of rhetoric at the Collège Louis-le-Grand in Paris on Aug. 16, 1716, Aug. 24, 1715, and Aug. 17, 1715. "Oratoriae institutiones" contains instructions for oratory, discussing such topics as composition; tropes such as synecdoche, metonymy, metaphor, irony, and  litotes; uses of allegory, hyperbole, and repetition; presentation of an argument through definition, enumeration, comparison, juxtaposition, and opposition; and the effects of the speaker's voice and gestures, his choice of ending, and his reading or reciting from memory. Sections of historical examples follow, entitled "Variae amplificationes", and "Variae varus de argumentis historiae."  There are two long unsigned poems: "Septhias sive innocens victima"; and "Ignorantiae regnum carmen."  Finally, there are math lessons on algebra and numbers, fractions, and proportions.

desc: Copy, dated 1800 in Ocotlán, owned by Father Juan Francisco Torralba of the province of San Ypólito Mártir of the city of Oaxaca, of an anonymous Zapotec grammar and confessionary, probably written sometime after 1666. The first 48 leaves contain a grammar in Spanish of the Zapotec language, including notes on pronunciation; explanations of the various parts of a sentence; verb conjugations; and extensive discussion of dipthongs and particles.  Also included are sections on numbers and ways of counting in Zapotec; and Spanish-Zapotec glossaries for parts of the body, kinship terms, and names of towns.  The liturgical texts for administering the sacraments of baptism, communion, last rites, and marriage are given in Spanish and Zapotec, arranged in double columns on each page, as is the "Confessonario zaapoteco del valle," with questions and responses based on each of the Ten Commandments. Also included are glossaries of nouns and verbs listed according to conjugation; dialogues of common phrases in Zapotec; and a second confessionary from the village of Santa María Petapa. Additional notes at the end of the ms. list deaths of parishioners in various villages from 1786-1798; and accounts of parish revenues from tithes, and expenses for masses.

title: Title page and introductory note by Antonio de Morga to the second volume of his compilation of cédulas, Segundo tomo de recopilación de cédulas, 1633 June 10.
creator: Quito (Audiencia). Presidente (1616-1636 : Morga)$$QQuito (Audiencia). Presidente (1616-1636 : Morga)
desc: Photostatic reproduction of title page and introduction by Antonio de Morga to the second volume of his compilation of cédulas, Segundo tomo de recopilación de cédulas. In order to provide governors and judges, both now and in the future, with a record of all the royal cédulas that have been issued by the king and the Consejo de Indias pertaining to the Audiencia of Quito, and so that they can see the decrees which were originally handed down, added, revoked, and modified, Morga, president of the Audiencia, ordered that they be copied and compiled into volumes, arranged by subject for easy access.  Morga also ordered a certified copy of all the ordinances of the Audiencia to be included in the volumes, as the originals were torn and in poor condition.  The introductory note to the compilation of cédulas is signed by Morga and dated June 10, 1633 in Quito. The title leaf of the second volume contains a listing of the cédulas issued to the Audiencia between 1589 and 1632, with page numbers for each year.

Ayer MS 1327.$$QNewberry Library. | Exposición general de las islas Filipinas (1887 : Madrid, Spain)$$QExposición general de las islas Filipinas
desc: Catalog, dated March 5, 1887 in Manila, of objects pertaining to the religion and culture of the Igorrotes, which were placed on display at the Exposición general de las islas Filipinas held in Madrid, Spain in 1887. The 141 display items document the culture and way of life of the 500,000 Philippine Igorrotes, members of the Malay racial group who occupy an extensive area of the island of Luzón including the provinces of Abra, Cagayan, Isabela, Nueva Vizcaya, Ilocos, La Unión, and Pangasinan. Entries contain display numbers, native names, origens, and descriptions of such items as clay figures used in religious worship; ceremonial chairs occupied by chieftains and their wives; dishes and plates, with notes on the foods prepared by the Igorot; drinking gourds; cane and bamboo baskets; loincloths, turbans, and other articles of clothing; necklaces made of glass beads and pieces of flint; amulets; backpacks, musical instruments, and boats. The catalog also describes knives, daggers, bows and arrows, and axes, as well as various products especially cultivated by the Igorot such as rice, honey, dates, cotton, and tobacco.

title: Journal et nottes [!] du voyage aux ruines del Palenque années 1832,33  / par Jean Frederic Waldeck.
creator: Waldeck, Frédéric de, 1766-1875.$$QWaldeck, Frédéric de
desc: Waldeck's transcription of his notes on his travels and research in Palenque and the Yucatán between 1832 and 1836 (some of which may also be found in his Journal No. 24), with some changes, additions, and deletions. Waldeck describes the architecture and construction of Mayan structures at Palenque--temples, palaces, towers, houses, and pyramids--analyzing their relief sculptures, medallions, niches, and large figures.  Throughout the notes he reflects on the origin and nature of the Mayan civilization, and refers to related drawings by including the corresponding plate numbers.  There is also an inventory of drawings he completed after he left Mexico in 1837, and a chapter on natural history, dealing with the physical aspects of the Indians and with the animals and insects he encounters.  Waldeck includes population charts, glossaries, and newspaper clippings.  The final section, dated 1837, in Paris, contains an explanation of a manuscript from the University of Mexico on the migration of the Mexican Indians; notes on the similarities between ancient Mexican art and mythology and that of Egypt and Babylonia; and comments of Sept. 23, 1853 on a visit with J.L. Stephens, author of Incidents of travel in the Yucatán, and engraver Frederick Catherwood.

desc: Ms. ledger record for the town of Salisbury Town, Sangamon County, Ill., containing entries for April 2, 1878-April 13, 1926. Record book contains minutes of monthly meetings, signed by various town clerks; meetings of auditors, highway commissioners, supervisors, election board, and board of health; and court records, financial statements, and other records. desc: Unsigned 6-part historical summary, dated 1835? of the piracy, seizure and destruction of Spanish property perpetrated by the Moros, from the times of the first colonial settlements in 1564 to 1806, including a description of past and current measures adopted by the government to pacify the Moros, as well as proposals for waging a more effective campaign against them. Commissioned by the Sociedad Económica of the Philippines, of which he is a member, the author recounts early Spanish confrontations with the Moros, emphasizing their unrelenting resistance to the imposition of colonial rule.  The author sees the Spaniards' early abandonment of Joló island to the Moros in 1658 as a principal cause of the hostilities which have continued into the 19th century. In addition, the Portuguese and the Dutch have furthered their own ends in the power struggle with Spain by exploiting the latter's campaigns against the Moros, and by selling weapons to the Moros. Part 3 covers the years between 1779 and 1792, and describes various Spanish forts in the Visayans and elsewhere; the status of their weapons, artillery, and manpower; and types and numbers of boats used in military operations. Part 4 outlines government measures and money spent to pacify the Moros, from 1793 to 1796, during the early years of the administration of governor Aguilar. desc: Documents, including reports, appointments, orders, letters, inventories, and accounts, from 1767-1781, concerning the expulsion of the Jesuits from Mexico in 1767, and the confiscation of their property and holdings. Viceroy Croix's signed order of June 12, 1767 names Machado Fiesco as secretary to the visitor general, Joseph de Gálvez, and authorizes him to execute orders for the expulsion of the Jesuits.  Croix's signed instructions, dated June 16, 1767, outline procedures to be followed by the commissioners named to carry out the royal expulsion decree of February 27, 1767. The bulk of the papers, dating from June 27-Oct. 6, 1767, are reports signed by Machado, describing the deportation of Jesuits and appropriation of property from the 5 Jesuit colegios in Puebla.  Soldiers are sent to the colegios and to the outlying Jesuit-owned haciendas to round up the priests, who are taken under military escort by Captains Francisco Echeagary and Antonio Rodríguez to Jalapa and then to Veracruz for the voyage to Europe.  Included in the reports are lists of the names of the expelled priests and room-by-room inventories of their personal belongings; inventories of the haciendas, ranchos, houses, and other land holdings of the Jesuits; lists of provisions, supplies, sums of money, and clothing confiscated from the colegios; and financial statements of income and outstanding debts of the colegios. title: Papers pertaining to the history and antiquities of Chiapas, Mexico, 1897-1909.
creator: León, Nicolás, 1859-1929.$$QLeón, Nicolás
desc: Research papers and letters, dating from 1897-1909, relating to the history of Chiapas, and containing a partial draft of León's proposed Ensayo de una historia general del estado de Chiapas. The scrapbook contains research notes from other published works on Chiapas and on Palenque in particular, such as Thompson's Ancient tombs of Palenque, Gunckel's Analysis of the day signs in the Palenquen inscriptions; and Holmes' Archaeological studies.  There are sketches in watercolor and pencil of Indian motifs; architectural drawings and ground-plans of temples; printed illustrations of works by Waldeck and Del Río; newspaper clippings; and photographs of the Palenque ruins, Indians of Chiapas, and numerous bishops of the province.  The draft is entitled Ensayo de una historia general del estado de Chiapas / por el Dr. Nicolás León, and covers the first five sections of the first part of his proposed outline. León discusses the pre-Columbian geography of Chiapas, as well as the various Indian tribes of the area, their history and their languages.  In addition to descriptions of the gods with their Indian names, he includes lists of words and numbers and translations of the Pater Noster in native languages of Chiapas such as Chañabal, Chiapaneco, Chol, Mame, Maya Quiché, Tzotzil, Tzendal, Lacandon, and Zoque. title: Noticias de la nueva California
creator: Palóu, Francisco, 1723-1789.$$QPalóu, Francisco
desc: A copy, made in 1792, by Father Manuel de Vega of the Convento de San Francisco in Mexico, of Palóu's history of Upper California and the Franciscan missions with which he was associated from 1768 to 1783. Pt. 1 is an account of the missions of Old or Baja California which were entrusted to Franciscans such as Palóu, Juan Crespí, and Junípero Serra, when the Jesuits were expelled from Mexico in 1767.  Between 1768 and 1773, Palóu served as head of San Xavier and as business manager for the expeditions of Gálvez and Portolá to Upper California, gathering and forwarding supplies to the new settlements.  In 1773, the Dominicans were given control of all the missions in Baja California, and the Franciscans moved on to work in Upper California.  Pts. 2, 3, and 4 deal with the founding of San Diego, Monterey, San Luis Obispo, San Gabriel, and San Francisco, and the problems of hostile Indians, disease, lack of provisions, locusts, and floods faced by the missionaries; the movement of supply ships up and down the coast; and the explorations northwards to Canada and Alaska.  Palóu includes Crespí's diaries of the Portolá expedition to Monterey of 1769-1770; the Fages expedition to San Francisco of 1772; and the Pérez expedition to British Columbia of 1774; as well as letters of Father Serra to Viceroy Bucareli regarding Monterey.  Palóu's status report to the viceroy on the 5 Monterey missions provides a description of each mission, its population, its harvests, and numbers of births

title: [Early Spanish land contracts and other archival documents] [between 1416 and 1777].
desc: Archival records from Andalucía--principally Córdoba and Seville--dated between 1416 and 1777, including land sale contracts, annuities, wills, and litigation and nobility papers. Most of the documents are "cartas de censo", special contracts in which the owner of property--generally farm land including olive groves, vineyards, mills and olive presses--transfers his rights of possession to another person or body in exchange for a specified censo (tax or tribute) to be paid as specified. Many of the "cartas de censo" included here transfer property rights to convents, monasteries, or other bodies, such as the military order of Alcántara, the revenues from which are to be used to say masses or provide a church burial for the donor.  There are also wills, an inventory of dowry goods and property, lists of repairs and improvements made to farms, litigation papers involving conveyance and inheritance of land titles, land sale and lease contracts, payment receipts, and petitions for nobility status, and for membership in the Orden de Santiago. Seville, Córdoba, and Toledo are the areas most frequently mentioned, although some documents concern property in Cádiz, Granada, Málaga, Baena, Utrera, Osuna, Alcala de Guadaira, La Rambla, Segovia, Cardeña, Montilla, Jerez de la Frontera, and Barbará in Tarragona. The autograph signature of King Philip V of Spain appears on the announcement, dated Dec. 30, 1744, to the council and officials of Velez of the marriage of his daughter,

title: Indian incidents [between 1873 and 1875]  / in the handwriting of the late Sam[ue]l G. Drake, Indian historian & antiquary ...
creator: Drake, Samuel G., 1798-1875.$$QDrake, Samuel G.
desc: Drake's transcriptions, with editorial comment, of fourteen copies of a "News-Letter" supplied to him by John A. Lewis.  The newsletters contain eyewitness narratives and other documents mainly relating to seventeenth and eighteenth century Indian captivities, wars, peace negotiations, etc., extracted from a variety of printed and other sources. They document Maj. John Doughty's expediton to the Chickasaw and battle on the Tennessee River (1790); peace negotiations between Alexander McGillivray of the Creeks and Edward Telfair of Georgia (1790); a massacre of captive Indians at Marblehead, Mass. (1677); the capture of Baron de Graffenried (North Carolina Palatines) and John Lawson by the Tuscarora Indians (1711); the captivity of Pennsylvania widow Massy Harbison (1792); Missouri Indian revenge upon a French Louisiana trader (1741); Conrad Weiser's embassy to the Iroquois (1745); events leading up to a Maine Indian massacre (1749), etc.

desc: Fragment of a village land book with two pages of text and picture captions in Nahuatl, created during the first half of the 18th century, probably between 1700-1743, documenting land claims in the village of Tepotzotlán. A village book compiled by the Nahuas to describe their lands and to guarantee their rights of ownership before Spanish administrators, the Codex records the names, acreage, and boundaries of the districts belonging to the village of Tepotzotlán.  It also identifies the principal private landowners of the town, and includes their portraits and quantity of land | owned.  Christian settlements are depicted throughout the Codex with drawings of churches, as well as the "tecpan" or city hall; magueys and nopals indicate the principal crops cultivated in the area.  Circles represent units of land measurement in "mecatls," and houses indicate the number of tribute-payers in each district.

title: Parabolas y exemplos sacados de la naturaleza y de los costumbres del campo aplicados á la moral cristiana  / obra escrita en lengua zapoteca para el consuelo e instrucción de los naturales de la misma lengua por el R.P. M. Fray Pedro de la Cueba de la Orden de Predicadores.
creator: Cueva, Pedro de la, d. 1611.$$QCueva, Pedro de la
desc: Photographic reproduction of a compilation of parables and moral lessons in Zapotec by the Dominican Father Pedro de la Cueva, probably written around 1600. Examples from nature and local customs are used to teach the Zapotec Indians moral and spiritual principles of Christianity. For example, Christ is compared to the sower, and his divine teachings are the seeds planted in the fertile soil of the heart of the virtuous man.  Other moral lessons are based on comparisons with such examples as the loyal mastiff, the steed which must be controlled, the falcon, the spider, and the farmer who protects his crops from birds and animals.

The compilation of the Glossa ordinaria was undertaken in northern France around 1100, principally by Anselm of Laon, with the assistance of his brother Ralph; and Gilbert of Auxerre (probably responsible for the gloss of the Gospel of Luke), with commentaries for every book of the Bible available by around 1135.  Leaves [1] and [2] contain chapter summaries and a preface to the reader, with Biblical text and gloss on leaves [3]-[83]. (For additional information on Biblical glosses, cf. Christopher de Hamel's Glossed books of the Bible and the origins of the Paris booktrade. Woodbridge [England] : D.S. Brewer, 1984).

title: [Liber epilogorum in gesta sanctorum], [approximately 1250].
creator: Bartholomew, of Trent, -approximately 1251.$$QBartholomew
desc: Legendary of saints, composed in 1244 by the Dominican Fra Bartolomeo da Trento, at the Monastery of San Lorenzo in Trento, Italy, and probably transcribed around 1250 in northern Italy. The legendary is arranged according to the liturgical year from Advent to the Feast of the Dedication of the Church, ending with the lives of Saints Josaphat and Barlaam. Unlike earlier compilations of the lives of the saints, intended to be read during meals in the refectory or at Divine Office, Fra Bartolomeo's Liber epilogorum was written for private use, and for use by preachers as a source of examples for their sermons.

creator: Miller, Helen Miner, creator.$$QMiller, Helen Miner
desc: Includes records dating back to 1888, assembled and saved by Wisconsin Winnebago Business Committee official Helen Miner Miller. Records document the process of organizing the tribe under the Indian Reorganization Act of 1934, and the governance and welfare of the tribe during the middle decades of the 20th century. There are also tribal newsletters, periodicals, writings and reports concerning the Wisconsin Winnebago. Three microfilm reels contain copies of Wisconsin Winnebago Business Committee files. Historical documents obtained to support the 1960s tribal organization under the Indian Reorganization Act include a 1901 Wisconsin Winnebago annuity payroll, 1910 census rolls for both the Wisconsin and Nebraska Winnebago with related correspondence, 1913 materials relating to the census rolls and the division of the Winnebago fund, enrollment materials from 1936 and later, several Winnebago meeting minutes dating from 1935, materials related to housing and homesteads beginning in 1888, and a copy of the Indian Reorganization Act of 1934. The process of organizing, tribal fact-finding, and governance is documented in the minutes of the Wisconsin Winnebago Business Committee, in tribal newsletters, and in documents files on the tribe's Constitution and Bylaws, elections, ordinances, land ownership and lost lands, finances, etc. There are also records of efforts to obtain and divide the U.S. Claims Commission settlement for ceded lands, and to procure and administer two 1960s g

Time and again the tribe was challenged by loss of ancestral land, disease, forced removals, and poverty. Under the 1837 Treaty the Winnebago ceded all their land east of the Mississippi. As a result of that treaty, the Winnebago became a wandering people. They were relocated numerous times from southern Minnesota, Iowa, South Dakota, and finally to Nebraska. A group of Winnebago families went back to Wisconsin and homesteaded land along with their non-Indian neighbors. They formed the nucleus of what became the Ho-Chunk Nation of Wisconsin. The Winnebago remaining in Nebraska became the Winnebago Tribe of Nebraska. In 1949, the Nebraska and Wisconsin Winnebago joined forces to file a common claim before the U.S. Indian Claims Commission seeking payment on ceded lands. In Wisconsin, the group handling this issue assembled as the acting Wisconsin Winnebago Business Committee. By 1961, the acting Wisconsin Winnebago Business Committee began working to organize the Wisconsin Winnebago Tribe under Section 16 of the 1934 Indian Reorganization Act, and prepared a number of drafts resulting in the first Wisconsin Winnebago Tribal Constitution. The U.S. Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) undertook a census of tribal members to determine those eligible to vote in the first election under the reorganization. In this election, which took place on January 19, 1963, tribal members ratified the Constitution and Bylaws of the Wisconsin Winnebago Tribe with a vote of 514 for and 5 against. The documents were later approved by the Commissioner of Indian Affairs and the Assistant Secretary of the Interior. In a 1994 amended version of the Constitution, the Wisconsin Winnebago Tribe officially reverted to its original Siouan name, becoming the Ho-Chunk Nation of Wisconsin. title: Albert M. MacDonald travel journal : manuscript.
creator: MacDonald, Albert M., creator.$$QMacDonald, Albert M.
desc: Unbound travel journal of Albert M. MacDonald, detailing vacation trips he took with family from their home in Cleveland, Ohio, to locations on the east coast of the United States and elsewhere, between 1937 and 1951. He covers three summer vacations in detail. During the first trip (7-22 August 1937), MacDonald and family visited Whiteface Mountain, Lake Placid, and Fort Ticonderoga in New York. Durning the second trip (3-19 August 1940), MacDonald drove through Upstate New York, including Niagara Falls, and up the coast of New England, passing through Boston, various locations in Maine (including Bangor, Portland, and Wyman Dam), and Burlington, Vermont, from which the family took a ferry ride. MacDonald and family then spent several days at a cottage with friends on Owasco Lake in Cayuga County, New York, where they swam, paddled canoes, and visited Taughannock Falls. The third trip (23-29 August 1941) was further south in Washington, D.C. and Virginia. MacDonald and family spent time sightseeing in Washington before driving to Mount Vernon and Monticello. They also drove through Shenandoah National Park on Skyline Drive and the the Blue Ridge Mountains. The travelogue of these three automobile trips is illustrated with both snapshots and commercially issued photographs of the areas that MacDonald and family visited. title: Diary of Mrs. Algeline Jackson Ashley crossing the Plains in 1852, [ca. 1930?].
creator: Ashley, Algeline Jackson, b. 1830.$$QAshley, Algeline Jackson
desc: Typescript, dated before 1937, of a portion of the diary kept by Algeline Jackson Ashley on her journey to California across the Great Plains between May 7 and June 23, 1852. Mrs. Ashley and her husband, William Ashley, depart from Hanesville [Wisconsin?] on May 7, 1852.  However, the portion of the diary transcribed here picks up the account on May 29, mid-way through the journey, just after the wagon train has left Ft. Laramie, Wyoming. Their route takes them through Wyoming and Utah, through the Black Hills, along the Platte River, the Green River, Ft. Bridger, and Echo Creek.  The last entry, dated June 23, 1852, finds the group driving through Salt Lake City, Utah, having been on the trail for 47 days.  Mrs. Ashley includes her observations on the Indians they encounter; the hardships the pioneers endure such as steep, rocky terrain, poisonous water, and lack of grass for the horses, and illnesses such as measles and mountain fever; and the landscapes along the way which she finds so beautiful.  She displays a great knowledge and love of plants and trees in her entries which describe the native plants and trees she sees: greasewood, flowering currants, cedar, moss, Norway pine, larkspur, pinks, balm, cherry trees, purple and orange flowering peas, sage, prickly pears, flowering bunch beans, and mosses.

title: Diaries 1858 Jan. 1-1866 Dec. 31.
creator: Wing, John M. (John Mansir), 1845-1917.$$QWing, John M.
desc: Nine pocket diaries containing entries by book collector and newspaperman, John M. Wing, for the years 1858 to 1866. Wing was an avid journal writer, almost unfailingly making an entry for each day of the year in his diary which he considered to be "a useful book", "the best companion that adversity gives", "a true friend, a secret counselor".  He began keeping a diary in 1858, when he was only thirteen years old, and the early journals from 1858-1862 contain his observations on weather, dinners and meetings with friends, classes and homework assignments at the Pulaski Academy in Pulaski, N.Y. where he was a student, and his experiences setting type and working in the print shop of the Pulaski Democrat. The diaries also contain miscellaneous quotes jotted down from Latin authors, Shakespeare, and other poets; for example, the 1861 diary begins with a patriotic Civil War poem (by Wing?) attacking "Jeff Davis" and the "traitors" who need to be taught to "obey the Constitution", and ends with Wing's pen sketch of Davis on the gallows. In addition, the 1862 and 1863 diaries contain a small pocket in which Wing kept numerous small newspaper clippings of interest, collection receipts, business cards, and short pencilled notes. Beginning in 1863, as Wing continued his newspaper career in the Rome office of the Utica Evening Telegraph, the entries became progressively longer and more detailed, and often included Wing's accounts of his newspaper subscription collections. creator: Catholic Church.$$QCatholic Church.
desc: Illustrated ms. prayer-book, owned by Juan Balthasar de Loaysa y Chaves, canon of the cathedral of Segovia, and member of the coordinating Consejo de Inquisición, possibly written in Segovia in 1761, or shortly thereafter. Contains prayers for days of the week and special occasions, hand-written in red and black, with 154 engraved scenes from the life and passion of Christ. Prayers include "Acto de contrición", to be recited before saying the rosary; "Mysterios gozosos" to be recited Mondays and Thursday, consisting of the mysteries of the Annunciation, Visitation of St. Elizabeth, the Nativity, Presentation in the Temple, and Christ teaching the church elders; "Mysterios dolorosos", for Tuesdays and Fridays, consisting of mysteries of Christ praying in Gethsemane, receiving the crown of thorns, carrying the cross, and the crucifixion; and "Misterios gloriosos" for Wednesdays and Saturdays, or mysteries of the Resurrection, Ascension, Pentecost, Assumption and Coronation of the Virgin; and the Litany of the Virgin.

title: De exaudibili & efficacissima or[ati]one corporis & animae saluberrimo medicami[n]e [tractatus] / [between 1510 and 1529?]. / quem Antonius Gazius Patauus Artium & Medicinae Professor minimus ad dei Laudem & pro fidelium salute ex diuino[rum] scriptu[rum] dictis compilauit,
creator: Gazio, Antonio, 1449-1528.$$QGazio, Antonio
desc: Ms. book of prayers and meditations, dated 1496 in Venice, by Antonio Gazio, a prominent Padua physician; and transcribed sometime after 1496, probably in Italy--possibly Venice--between 1510 and 1529. Text, arranged in 60 chapters, is devoted to the theory and practice of prayer, reflecting Gazio's ideas on the benefits of daily prayer and meditation for both spiritual and corporal well-being. He discusses the need for prayer; how to pray effectively; and includes prayers in each chapter.  His text is full of references to the writings of Church fathers and to classical philosophers, such as Saints Augustine, Gregory, Bernard, Paul, and John Chrysostom; Petrus de Palude, patriarch of Jerusalem, Plato, Aristotle, Isidoro de Sevilla, and Alcibiades.

desc: Occult commonplace book mainly compiled by Robert Ashley. First section (foliated leaves 4r-38v) written by Ashley includes charms, spells, ritual magic, and medical recipes. Second section inverted and beginning on opposite end with prayers, charms, lists of saints is in red, green and black ink, and rudimentary table of contents, mostly in Latin, some text in Ashley's hand.

title: L'art de fortifier les places regulières et irregulières expliqué, pratiqué, et demonstré d'une façon sensible et aggreable, [ca. 1655].
creator: Bourdin, Pierre, 1595-1653.$$QBourdin, Pierre
desc: Unsigned ms., possibly from around 1655, of Pierre Bourdin's "L'Architecture militaire", printed in Paris by Guillaume Benard in 1655. Preceding the main text is a glossary of fortification terms, entitled "Table des pieces, noms, et termes propres a l'art de fortifier," which explains such terms as "redoubt", "parapet", "glacis", "talus", "coping", and "embankment."  Bourdin then proceeds to discuss the geometric forms of fortified structures, such as the four-, five-, and six-sided star ("étoile"), and the half-moon ("demi-lune"), and compares the French, Italian, and Dutch styles of fortification.

Ayer Manuscript Collection (Newberry Library)$$QEdward E. Ayer Manuscript Collection (Newberry Library) | Newberry Library. Manuscript. Ayer MS 1824.$$QNewberry Library.
desc: Drawings of 63 figures of the Codex Mendoza, with explanations translated into French. The drawings follow, in part, those found in the Codex Mendoza, an early Aztec pictorial work commissioned by Antonio de Mendoza, first viceroy of New Spain from 1535-1550, for presentation to Charles V, and now in the Bodleian Library.  There are three parts as they are laid out in the original Codex: the first presents a chronology of the Aztec kings from 1324 to 1521, indicating the number of years each king ruled, and which villages he conquered.  The second part is a detailed inventory of the tributes that each town and village was obliged to pay to the Emperor.  The third part describes the life of the Aztecs from birth, their economy, customs, laws and punishments.

title: Quaker marriage certificate between John Bringhurst and Rosina Matern, 1682 June 2 : manuscript.
creator: Bringhurst, John, active 1680-1685, creator.$$QBringhurst, John
desc: Marriage certificate between John Bringhurst and Rosina Matern, certifying a wedding ceremony held during a Quaker meeting in London. The certificate is autographed by Bringhurst and Matern, as well as 44 Quaker men and 26 Quaker women who witnessed the wedding. Among the witnesses are several prominent printers and publishers of London and notable figures in Quaker history, including Andrew Sowle, successor of Bringhurst as printer of Quaker publications; Tace Sowle, daughter of Andrew and successor to his printing business; William Bradford, printer in colonial Pennsylvania and New York; and George Keith, a Quaker missionary who gained prominence in the Jersey provinces and Philadelphia area and later broke with the Quakers to establish a short-lived sect known as the Christian Quakers.

title: Theodore Thomas papers 1852-1926.
creator: Thomas, Theodore, 1835-1905.$$QThomas, Theodore
desc: Correspondence, mainly incoming, of Theodore Thomas and Rose Fay Thomas, photographs of musicians, and guestbook kept by Rose Fay Thomas. Most of the letters from well-known music and arts figures (many in German) relate to Thomas' tenure at the CSO; there are also drafts of Thomas' own letters, and some addressed after his death to Rose Fay Thomas.  Among the many prominent correspondents are Amy Beach, Daniel Burnham, John A. Carpenter, Edward Elgar, Robert Frost, Lilli Lehmann, I.J. Paderewski, and Piotr Tschaikowsky, and Richard Wagner.  Also cabinet photographs of twenty-eight composers, musicians, and performers including Brahms, Liszt, Paderewski, Ernestine Schumann-Heink, Edward Elgar, and Fannie Bloomfield Zeisler.  Begun in 1904, the guestbook is signed by visiting musicians, and other prominent individuals, and often includes musical notation, correspondence, and images of signers.

title: Sketchbook [between 1825 and 1852]
creator: Waldeck, Frédéric de, 1766-1875.$$QWaldeck, Frédéric de
desc: Sketchbook, probably begun by Waldeck in 1825 while travelling in Mexico, and continued through 1852, after he had returned to Europe, containing drawings of Indian ruins, antiquities, and other sites in central Mexico. The sketches, some of which are rough pencil outlines, and others detailed color drawings, document temples, pyramids, and carvings primarily in Xochicalco, near Cuernavaca, and a few sites in Papantla and Miacatlán, including the Miacatlán hacienda of Ángel Pérez Palacios, from whom Waldeck received a Nahuatl glyph map of the Tetlama region sometime between 1829 and 1831. In addition to architectural and figure studies, there are a few drawings of native flora and fauna, such as a coyote, eagle, and a tree enshrouded in vines. Another group of scientific diagrams relate to Waldeck's interest in optics--reflection, refraction, mirrors, and shadows.  Two pages in French, in Waldeck's hand, dated 1825 in Paris, contain his notes on the religions of India, illustrated with small sketches of Gaṇeśa, the elephant-faced Hindu deity. Also included are a watercolor sketch of the crucified Jesus held by his mother, and pencil drawings of sculptural figures, and historical figures in native dress.

desc: Catalog, dated March 5, 1887 in Manila, of objects pertaining to the religion and culture of the Igorrotes, which were placed on display at the Exposición general de las islas Filipinas held in Madrid, Spain in 1887. The 141 display items document the culture and way of life of the 500,000 Philippine Igorrotes, members of the Malay racial group who occupy an extensive area of the island of Luzón including the provinces of Abra, Cagayan, Isabela, Nueva Vizcaya, Ilocos, La Unión, and Pangasinan. Entries contain display numbers, native names, origens, and descriptions of such items as clay figures used in religious worship; ceremonial chairs occupied by chieftains and their wives; dishes and plates, with notes on the foods prepared by the Igorot; drinking gourds; cane and bamboo baskets; loincloths, turbans, and other articles of clothing; necklaces made of glass beads and pieces of flint; amulets; backpacks, musical instruments, and boats. The catalog also describes knives, daggers, bows and arrows, and axes, as well as various products especially cultivated by the Igorot such as rice, honey, dates, cotton, and tobacco.

title: Beschreibung der Ueberreste Aztekischer Niederlassungen auf ihrer Wanderung nach dem Thale von Mexico durch den gegenwärtigen Freistaat von Zacatecas : nach örtlichen Forschungen und Vermessungen zusammengestellt und durch das in Aztekischer Bilderschrift in Museum zu Mexico vorhandene Manuscript erläutert  / von Carl de Berghes.
creator: Berghes, Carl de, 1792-1869.$$QBerghes, Carl de
desc: Berghes' ms., written in Münsterpumpe bei Stolberg, Germany, in 1855 (although some of the drawings are dated 1832 and 1834), describes the ruins of the settlements left by the Aztecs in their wanderings in the valley of Mexico (now the state of Zacatecas), from the legendary Aztlán to Tenochtitlán between 1116 and 1325.  Accompanying his descriptions and historical background are 21 plates of maps, site and floor plans, and finely-detailled drawings in pen-and-ink and watercolor of the buildings, pyramids, terrain, and carved figures found in the ruins at La Quemada.  With his discussion of the Sombrerete ruins are a map of the site and sketches of the surrounding Cerro de los Bueyes.  He also includes drawings of the mountains in Tula, as well as an Aztec calendar wheel and several portraits of Indians from Zacatecas. Finally, there is a copy of the Códice Boturini, a pictorial history of the Aztec migration, copied by Berghes in 1832 from the original maguey ms. in the National Museum of Anthropology in Mexico City, with Berghes' ms. notes added in German.

title: Speaking our selves : new plays by African women  / edited by Asiimwe Deborah Kawe and Robert H. Vorlicky ; foreword by Esi Sutherland-Addy.
creator: Kawe, Asiimwe Deborah.$$QKawe, Asiimwe Deborah.
desc: Speaking Our Selves brings together eight remarkable plays by women writers from the under-represented African countries of Tanzania, Mozambique, Ethiopia, Mali, Burundi, Benin, and Sudan, plus a play by award-winning Ugandan playwright and volume coeditor Asiimwe Kawe. Four of the plays are translated into English from Kiswahili, French, or Kirundi and French, while most of the plays preserve African indigenous languages, including Runyankore, Lusoga, Mina, Fon, Bambara, Luganda, Kiswahili, and Kirundi. Although the plays are united in presenting women as central figures who own their voices, they also represent a rich diversity of story-telling. Each unique dramaturgy is rooted in African forms of story-telling that occasionally merge with recognizable Western forms to create hybrid, dramatic forms. These hybrid methods emphasize the striking ways in which African women writers continue to experiment with form, moving beyond Western-influenced dramaturgy if and when it jeopardizes their authentic ways of artistic expression and creation through language, movement, and music, centered in African Cosmology. The plays within Speaking Our Selves confront a range of ideas and issues, including women embracing the potential of agency in often contested subject positions; confronting their historical object positions in worlds of devastating patriarchal authority; resisting toxic masculinity and persistent, oppressive binaries of gender roles; finding power in communities of women

desc: Photographic reproductions of three Mexican pictorial manuscripts--one from the late 16th century, the other two from the first half of the 18th century--concerning villages and lands in Tlaxcala and the valley of Mexico. The first ms., possibly dating from 1597, is a pictorial map with Nahuatl glosses, showing properties in the vicinity of Santa Barbara Tamascolco, including two churches, a river, four people, and various place glyphs.  Glosses mention Santa Barbara, Santa Ana, don Antonio de Mendoza, and Diego Muñoz, the Indian governor.  The other two documents are Techialoyan codices (nos. 717 and 716), fragments of village land books intended to legally establish the boundaries of a particular village, its barrios and outlying areas, and ownership claims to various land parcels. Illustrations, accompanied by explanatory texts in Nahuatl, the Indian language used in legal documents, depict the church, river, and farmlands of the village of San Pablo Huyxoapan, near Azcapotzalco, in what is now the Distrito Federal; individual fields are shown with their crops of maguey. In addition, the Santiago Chalco Codex contains illustrations of birds and animals, as well as a scene of the pueblo's patron saint being carried atop a trestle by the natives.

title: [Black Horse ledger] [ca. 1877-1879].
creator: Black Horse (Cheyenne)$$QBlack Horse (Cheyenne) | Edward E. Ayer Manuscript Collection (Newberry Library)$$QEdward E. Ayer Manuscript Collection (Newberry Library) | Newberry Library. Manuscript. Ayer MS 3227.$$QNewberry Library.
desc: Cheyenne ledger book, probably illustrated between 1877 and 1879, containing drawings by Black Horse and other Cheyenne warrior artists of scenes of warfare, hunting, and courtship. The Black Horse ledger book forms part of the long tradition of the Plains Indians of chronicling their lives pictorially, first on buffalo hides, and later, between 1865 and 1935, on the blank pages of ledger books obtained from U.S. soldiers, traders, missionaries, and reservation employees.  Warriors who fought in both the Northern and Southern Plains contributed drawings to this ledger, which depict Cheyenne attacks on Pawnee, Shoshone, Crow, and Snake Indians--both men and women; and encounters with white Army soldiers, and white settlers, some taking place inside houses, and possibly dating from 1878, when young men from Little Wolf and Morning Star's people were raiding during the flight home from the south.  Pages 22-23 contain a scene with caption "Cheyenne camp attacked at Powder River by soldiers (Mackenzies). Fall of 1876". Another drawing documents the 1874 attack near the Washita River on a wagon train under the escort of Major Lyman of the 5th Infantry. In addition to scenes of violent warfare, drawings of elk hunting and courtship are included.

title: Letter from Francisco, conde de Cabarrús, to Manuel de Godoy, duque de la Alcudia : manuscript, 1792 November 21-22.
creator: Cabarrús, Francisco, conde de, 1752-1810, author.$$QCabarrús, Francisco
desc: Copy of a letter sent from Francisco, conde de Cabarrús, to Manuel de Godoy, duque de la Alcudia and principe de la Paz, regarding the sender's imprisonment. Cabarrús rose quickly to prominence in the world of finance in Spain, becoming one of the founders of the Banco de San Carlos, the first national bank in Spain, in 1782. His success provoked the enmity of prominent government figures, including the conde de Lerena, Minster of Finance from 1785 to 1791. The conde de Lerena accused him of embezzlement in the bank and other financial improprieties, which led to his imprisonment. During this time, Cabarrús was also being investigated by the Inquisition for his opinions. The letter is composed primarily of a copy of a memorial to King Carlos IV, defending himself against the accusations and making his case that he had been wrongly imprisoned over the past 29 months.

title: Carta executoria a pedimento de Alvar Gonçalez vezino de la villa de Campanario, 1567 Jan. 27.
creator: Goncalez el Moxo, Alvar, active 1560-1567.$$QGoncalez el Moxo, Alvar
desc: Ms. patent of nobility, granted to Alvar Gonçalez el Moxo in Granada on Jan. 27, 1567. In the customary manner, Gonçalez presents his petition for status as an "hidalgo" to the "alcaldes de los hijos dalgo", the clerk of the province of León, and then to the president and judges of the Audiencia de Granada.  Witnesses in support of his request offer their testimony, including several neighbors: Francisco Gómez, Francisco Benítez, Gaspar Sánchez el Viejo, Pedro Muñoz el Viejo, Juan Sánchez de Martín Sánchez, and Elvira Rodríguez. Mary Eliza McDowell was born on 30 November 1854 to Malcolm and Jane Welch Gordon McDowell in Cincinnati, Ohio. After the American Civil War, in which McDowell's father served, the family moved to Chicago. Her father opened a steel rolling mill there, and the family joined the Methodist Church. McDowell became involved in various relief efforts and religious activities during her early years in Chicago. She took the lead in relief efforts after the Great Chicago Fire in 1871, and was later recognized by President Rutherford B. Hayes for her service. McDowell also organized religious classes for young people that attracted prominent figures in the temperance movement. She began her career working for Frances Williard, founder of the Women's Christian Temperance Movement. Soon, McDowell began to teach kindergarten classes at Hull House, founded by Jane Addams and Ellen Gates Starr. In 1894, the University of Chicago, working with the university's Christian Union, Jane Addams, and Professor J. Laurence Laughlin, established the University of Chicago Settlement in the Stock Yard District. The university hired McDowell to head a larger Back of the Yards settlement house, one of a colony of houses spread throughout the ethnically diverse immigrant neighborhood. McDowell opened the University of Chicago Settlement House to alleviate the crowded, unsanitary housing conditions that immigrant and African American families often faced. She organized classes, concerts, lectures, and clubs for men and women, including the Bohemian Women's Club and the Settlement Women's Club. Through her work, she began to feel that low wages correlated with a low standard of living and supported union organizing efforts to improve wages and working conditions. McDowell stood with workers during the stockyard strike in 1904 and urged unions to admit African Americans. For her efforts she received the nickname "Fighting Mary." McDowell worked with residents to improve their neighborhood through education and civic engagement. She worked with the suffrage movement to pressure city officials to clean up a rodent-infested garbage dump and the polluted waters of Bubbly Creek. McDowell also researched garbage collection methods for the Chicago Commission on Waste, established in 1913. In 1923, she became the Commissioner of Public Welfare under Mayor William Emmett Dever. McDowell helped to found the Women's Trade Union League of Chicago and lobbied the United States government to establish the Women's Bureau to study the living and working conditions of women and children in 1920. She died in Chicago on 14 October 1936 after suffering a stroke. | Purchase; Brad Emalfarb; 2022; 2022062799 | American social reformer active in the Chicago Set

Oswald Bruce Cooper (1879-1940) was one of the leading figures in American type design in the first half of the twentieth century. Born in Mount Gilead, Ohio and raised in Coffeyville, Kansas, Cooper left high school to work as a printer's apprentice and took correspondence courses in art. He came to Chicago in 1899 and studied at the Frank Holme School, where he also taught. Upon Holme's death in 1903, Cooper took over the affairs of the school, personally fulfilling the terms of its outstanding tuition contracts. In 1904, he partnered with Fred S. Bertsch in a lettering studio which, under the name Bertsch & Cooper, continued in business into the 1950s. In 1914 they added typesetting to their business. Their advertisements for clients like Marshall Field & Co. appeared widely in local print media, including the Chicago daily news; the firm also had wider exposure through Chicago-based clients who advertised nationally. Oswald Cooper's greatest influence was as the designer of a series of types for Barnhart Brothers & Spindler (the Chicago affiliate of the American Type Founders Co.). Those evidenced in the surviving papers are: Cooper Old Style (released 1919-1924); Cooper Black (1921); Cooper Black Italic (1922); Cooper Highlight (1922); Cooper Old Style Italic (1924); Cooper Black Condensed (1926); Dietz Text (circa 1927); Pompeian Cursive (1927); Boul Mich (1928-1929?); Cooper Fullface/Modern (1928-1929); and Cooper Fullface/Modern Italic (1928-1929). Cooper also designed an undated (and unreleased) sans serif; and in 1926-1927 Barnhart Bros. issued a series of "Ornaments, borders and screamers," a set of Christmas ornaments, and some ornamental initials by Cooper. Cooper Black became the largest selling single type face in the late 1920s and 1930s; it was the subject of a precedent-setting copyright lawsuit in 1926-1928. Cooper was a founding member of the 27 Chicago Designers and the Society of Typographic Arts, which produced a retrospective tribute to him, The book of Oz Cooper, in 1949. Cooper died on December 17, 1940. | Oswald Bruce Cooper Papers, The John M. Wing Foundation on the History of Printing, The Newberry Library, Chicago. | Organized into the following series: 1. title: El primer nueva coronica i bue[n] gobierno  / compuesto por don Phelipe Guaman Poma de Aiala, S[eñ]or. i P[ri]n[c]ipe.
creator: Guamán Poma de Ayala, Felipe, active 1613.$$QGuamán Poma de Ayala, Felipe
desc: Photographic reproduction of the Primer nueva coronica i buen gobierno, written to King Philip III by the Inca chronicler Guamán Poma de Ayala between 1583 and 1615. Guamán Poma's illustrated chronicle is divided into two books: the Nueva corónica and the Buen gobierno.  The first book, comprising fourteen chapters, includes the author's letters to the king and to the pope; his prologue to the readers; a Biblical account of the creation of the world; and descriptions of the Inca rulers and wives, the Inca system of laws and punishments, the native calendar, religious ceremonies, festivals, celebrations, and music, and the royal palaces, Inca nobles, and payments of tribute.  The second book contains  32 chapters, describing the conquest of Peru by Pizarro and Almagro; the death of Atalhuapa; the resistance of the Incas to colonization by the Spaniards; the viceroys of Peru; and colonial society and government.  There is also a description of colonial towns and cities.  Guamán Poma protests the destruction of traditional Inca society by the colonizers, and denounces the many abuses and injustices suffered by the Indians at the hands of the Spanish authorities and missionaries as they exploited the great mineral wealth of the country and attempted to Christianize the Incas. In an imaginary interview with the king, Guamán Poma questions the monarch about how the Indians are being treated, and presents his own conclusions and opinions on the subject.

title: Plan géometrîque et declaration des domaines du Chaigne Paroisse de Boyer appartenants a Dame Jeanne De Toisy, veuve du Sieur François Seriziat, négotiant, résidante en la Ville de Lyon / [1790]. / levé por Philibert Petit, Commissaire aux Rentes Emphitéoliques, résidant a Senecey le Chateau en 1790,
creator: Petit, Philibert.$$QPetit, Philibert.
desc: Ornately-calligraphed ms. land-use survey of 1790 of the estate of Jeanne De Toisy, widow of François Seriziat, located between Tournus and Chalon near Sennecey in Burgundy. The ms., drawn and signed by Philibert Petit, the local Commissaire aux Rentes, describes and measures 195 "ouvrées" of vineyards (an "ouvrée" is the amount of land a man can cultivate in one day), as well as other cultivated and wooded properties. The maps, drawn to scale, are labeled with the names of the tenant farmers, and indicate roads and communal land ("finage") as well.  Facing pages contain explanatory notes, number and sizes of the parcels, and list of buildings located on the property. The document may have been intended to indicate the precise apportionment of the production between the owners and tenants, or to determine tax assessments on the estate.

title: De monetis ponderibus & mensuris antiquorum [ca. 1712].
desc: Ms., probably compiled around 1712 by an anonymous Hebrew scholar from Toulouse, France, on the money, weights, and measures of the Greeks, Romans, and Hebrews. After a brief "praefatio" in Latin, the author explains that his work is a compilation of various authorities on the subject, from which he will derive certain conclusions and present them clearly to his readers. His principal sources include Bernard Lamy (1640-1715), Brian Walton (1600-1661), Edward Brerewood (1565?-1613), as well as a plethora of ancient writers such as Pliny, Plutarch, Flavius Josephus, St. Jerome, Guillaume Budé, Georg Agricola (1494-1555), and Isidore of Seville (d. 636). The text on money includes numerous tables listing the equivalent values of ancient money in contemporary English pounds and French coins, and a discussion of how the relationship of gold to silver has changed over the centuries.  The second section notes the different measures of weight used by ancient peoples, until the Roman Empire imposed its own systems of money and weight on its colonial subjects. The Hebrews have traditionally linked the concepts of money and weight, as seen in the names of their coins: "talent", "sicle", and "schekel". Forty pages of tables give the modern equivalents of Hebrew weights, the author having drawn largely from Flavius Josephus and Old Testament sources. The last section discusses the measurements of liquids and solids, relying on Lamy, Walton, Jacob Bontresius for Greek measures, the astron

title: Collection of land indentures and court orders involving properties and lands in Cornwall and Devon [ca. 1588]-1818.
desc: Land indentures and court orders concerning land disputes in England from the time of Elizabeth I, ca. 1588, to Sept. 26, 1818. Indentures document the sale, lease, mortgage, or transfer of houses, fields, pastures, orchards, meadows, mills, and outbuildings in various parishes in the counties of Devon and Cornwall, including property in Coryton, Druxton, Yeolmbridge, Lydford, Bratton Clovelly, and Little Torrington. Indenture no. 10, dated Feb. 20, 1683, grants Samuel Gilbert felling rights to timber trees on lands owned by Gabriel Gist. Two of the documents, one dated Nov. 29, 1731, and one dated Sept. 26, 1818, are court orders involving the litigation of land ownership disputes, issued by the justices of the Common Bench in the Court of Land Pleas in Westminster. Parties named in the indentures include John Wall, Anne and Thomas Sherwill, Ezekiel Wood, Henry Marten, Philip Welsh, Hugh Mill, Thomas Stert, Philip Stert, William Ouldbridge, and Elizabeth Prowse.

title: Ha nima vuh vae theologia yndorum rubinaam.
creator: Vico, Domingo de, 1485-1555.$$QVico, Domingo de
desc: Photographic reproduction of Theologia indorum in Cakchikel by Father Domingo de Vico and copied by Father Francisco Maldonado, probably from around 1671. The "theologia indorum" is based on events of the Old Testament, and was probably intended for use by missionary friars in teaching Christian theology to the Cakchikel Indians. The work begins with the story of Adam and Eve, and the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah, and also includes chapters on Biblical figures such as Abraham, Jacob, Joseph in Egypt, Kings David and Solomon, Job, Jonah, and Judith and Holofernes.

desc: An inventory of the supplies on hand in Mexico of gunpowder, saltpeter, and sulphur, as of April 30, 1768. A note indicates that the figures are taken from documents of the general accounting office of the gunpowder monopoly.

desc: Album amicorum of F.R.L. Gerstner, with inscriptions of friendship dated 1805-1833 from multiple family members and friends. Among the contributors are brother Ernst Gerstner of Helmstedt; cousins Joh. Wilh. Fricke and Friedrich Theodor Herrmann of Schöningen; brother-in-law G. Kühne; and friends W. Blanck of Ottleben, H. Kunkel of Gunsleben, Carl Bodenstein of Halberstadt, Heinrich Chr. Wilh. Overlach and J.H.C. Nolten of Helmstedt, Wilhelm Gebser of Gross-Bartensieben, and Betty Voigts, Betti Schmidt, Heinr. Friedr. Stätte, and G.F. Woldmann. At the beginning of the volume is a colored friendship vignette with the phrase "Das Liebe" and a four-line poem framed in gold foil. In the four corners of the page are pasted figures cut out from an engraving. Another page near the beginning also includes hand-colored figures cut from an engraving in the four corners, surrounding a cut-out, engraved image of a baptism. Affixed on several pages are decorative filigree cut-paper trees, flowers, garlands, and a friendship obelisk. Includes a partially completed index of the names of the inscribers.

title: Noticias relativas al estado de las Yslas Filipinas en el año de 1810
creator: Comyn, Tomás de.$$QComyn, Tomás de.
desc: An abridged version of Tomás de Comyn's Estado de las islas Filipinas en 1810, probably from around 1810, describing the status of the Philippine economy in 1810. Comyn, an agent for the Compañía de Filipinas, divides his study into sections on population, agricultural production, minerals, industry, principally textiles, and ownership of farms and landed estates.  There is also a brief history of the Real Compañía de Filipinas, founded in 1785 to develop commerce between Asia and America and Europe, and to stimulate growth of industry in the Philippines; and an analysis of sources of treasury revenues such as the state monopoly on tobacco, coconut wine and "nipa," betel, playing cards, cockfighting, and stamped paper; and "diezmos" or tithes. The first folded table contains population figures by province for "yndios" and mestizos, and comparative statistics for the years 1791 and 1810; the second one is a general balance sheet, based on figures for 1809, showing major government expenditures, revenues, and the current balance on hand. The author also discusses problems in the civil administration; ecclesiastical jurisdictions and dioceses; and the need to eliminate the Moro pirates on the islands of Mindanao, Basilán, and Joló.

desc: Four letters written between 1852 and 1862 by various government officials and political figures to José Fernando Ramírez, Mexican statesman, jurist, and scholar. In the May 1852 letter, José María Tornel, director of the College of Mining, informs Ramírez, head of the Museo Nacional, of the appointment of a curator of zoology for the museum.  Another 1852 letter is addressed to Ramírez at the Archivo General by José Miguel Arroyo, a secretary in the Department of Internal Relations, who explains that José María Tamariz has been hired at a monthly salary of 25 pesos to assist Ramírez in his work. Joaquín Velázquez de León, Minister of Development under Santa Ana, writes to Ramírez, now a magistrate of the Supreme Court, regarding monthly expenditures for salaries and operations of textile factories.  His letter of October 21, 1853 reports the figures sent to him by a textile manufacturer in Durango.  Finally, there is a brief letter, dated January 15, 1862, from Benigno Canto, an activist in Mexican political affairs, thanking Ramírez for his notes on three Indian painters.

title: [Prayer-book], [between 1470 and 1480].
creator: Benediktinerinnen-Abtei St. Walburg (Eichstätt, Germany)$$QBenediktinerinnen-Abtei St. Walburg (Eichstätt, Germany) | University of Illinois (Urbana-Champaign campus), joint owner.$$QUniversity of Illinois (Urbana-Champaign campus) | Newberry Library. Manuscript. Case MS 192.$$QNewberry Library.
desc: Prayer-book, probably copied by the Benedictine nuns of the Abbey of St. Walburga, overlooking Eichstätt in southern Germany, between 1470 and 1480. Not a Book of hours, this prayer-book was intended as an aid to spiritual devotion for simple, pious nuns of the cloister, and contains prayers for communion, Lent, and the Passion of Christ, as well as the Lord's Prayer, Mary Magdalene's prayers while she washed the feet of Christ, and prayers to Saint Brigit and Saint Anne, mother of the Virgin. Also included are prominent prayers to Saint Walburga, a local saint of the Eichstätt region.

title: Heures de la crois : Domine labia mea aperies et os meum annuntiab[i]t laudem tuam.
creator: Catholic Church.$$QCatholic Church.
desc: Book of hours according to the use of Thérouanne, probably copied and illuminated in the north of France around 1450. Calendar on first 6 leaves lists saints' days celebrated during each month.  Also included are the Hours of the Cross, Hours of the Holy Spirit, and Hours of the Virgin, consisting of Psalms, hymns, prayers, readings, and responses.  The Seven Penitential Psalms and the Litany of Saints were recited to ask for forgiveness for the dead.  Finally, Vigils, or Office, of the Dead contain prayers to be said over the coffin on the eve of the funeral Mass.

title: Executoria a pedimento de Rodrigo de Rueda vezino de la villa de Carmona contra el fiscal y co[n]cejo della, 1568 Dec. 3-1569 Feb. 7.
creator: Rueda, Rodrigo de, active 1553-1569.$$QRueda, Rodrigo de
desc: Ms. patent of nobility, dated Dec. 3, 1568 in Granada, granted to Luis, Bernardino, Rodrigo, and Baltasar de Rueda, brothers residing in Carmona (Seville, Spain). The petition is presented on Sept. 18, 1553 before the Audiencia judges and the "alcaldes de hijosdalgo" for the city of Carmona by Gonzalo Ruiz de Aguado, attorney for the Rueda brothers.  The state's attorneys in the case are Dr. Gaspar de Navarrete, "procurador fiscal", and Dr. Ramírez. Included in the text of the document are the 12 questions put to the witnesses summoned on behalf of the Ruedas: Juan de Lorca, Alonso Boga, and Cristóbal Martín, residents of Carmona; Fernando de Veas, constable of the town council of Carmona, Juan de Toledo, notary public of Carmona, and Juan de Marchena, cleric of the church of Santa María in Carmona. There is also a second, shorter interrogatory addressed to additional witnesses: Pero Sánchez de Sigüenza and Juan Pérez of Sigüenza; Fernán Sánchez Barbero of Villa Laín, and Sister María de Mendoza of the convent of Santa María de Belén. A preliminary judgment in favor of the Ruedas, dated Nov. 23, 1558 by Licenciados Gamboa, Mancanedo, and Diego de Zúñiga, is challenged in 1566, but reaffirmed May 6, 1567.  The "sentencia definitiva" or final decision is issued Dec. 3, 1568, and acknowledged and registered by town officials in Seville on Feb. 7, 1569.

desc: Processional, probably from mid- to late 13th c. for use by an Augustinian house in the diocese of Reims, probably the Abbaye Saint-Denis. The processional, not an "official" service book like the antiphonary or gradual, but created by singers for personal use, contains chants for Candlemas, Palm Sunday, and Rogationtide processions, and for those before Mass on Sundays and feast days. title: Collection of German baptismal Taufbriefe certificates, 1770-1831.
creator: Bitterlich, Carl August, printer.$$QBitterlich, Carl August | Cleve, G. D., printer.$$QCleve, G. D. | Hofmann, Carl Gotthilf, printer.$$QHofmann, Carl Gotthilf | Hofmann, Christian Gotthilf, printer.$$QHofmann, Christian Gotthilf | Röhm, Johann Traugott, printer.$$QRöhm, Johann Traugott | Schreibers Erben, printer.$$QSchreibers Erben
desc: Collection of German Taufbriefe, or folding baptismal certificates, most of which were printed in Saxony. All of the certificates are completed in manuscript, five by a godmother and three by a godfather, and dated in manuscript 1770-1831. Six of the certificates bear an imprint: Christian Gotthilf Hofman and Carl Gotthilf Hofman in Waldenburg, Schreibers Erben and G.D. Cleve in Leipzig, Johann Traugott Röhm in Saalfeld, and Carl August Bitterlich in Crottendorf. The two without imprints were probably printed in the same region within Saxony and Thuringia. The text of each certificate is letterpress-printed on one side of the sheet, while a different hand-colored paneled illustration (engraving, etching, or woodcut) is printed on the verso. Six of the designs have a central panel with a group of four figures, presumably representing the parents, priest, and godparent (alternately depicted as a man or woman) of the child being baptized. Another of the central designs depicts the baptism of Jesus Christ. The earliest certificate (dated 1770), bears 17 panels depicting the Creation, the Four Evangelists, and other biblical scenes, each with an engraved caption. The certificates are designed to be folded into a square like a letter. Some have remnants of the original red wax seals.

title: French library catalog written on playing cards : manuscript.
creator: Minot, Jean, active 1767-1808, contributor.$$QMinot, Jean | Purchase fund (in part). Society of Collectors (Newberry Library)$$QSociety of Collectors (Newberry Library)
desc: Deck of 52 playing cards repurposed as a manuscript card catalog, written in at least two hands, for a library or collection of French books, most of which were published between 1649 and 1812. On the verso of each card is an entry for one book, which includes shelfmark, title, author, place and date of publication, number of volumes, and bibliographic format or size. The format of the entries conforms to guidelines published in an early manual for systematizing catalog cards for libraries and book collections, Instruction pour procéder à la confection du catalogue de chacune des bibliothèques sur lesquelles les directoires ont dû ou doivent incessament apposer les scellés (Paris : De l'Imprimerie nationale, 1791), which recommends the use of repurposed playing cards. The cataloged books include histories, treatises, and works of literature. The playing cards where made by Parisian card maker Jean Minot, whose name "Minot" is printed on the Queen of Spades. Woodcut figures are printed on the face cards and hand colored with stencils; the numeral cards are stenciled with the symbols of their respective suits.

title: LeFlore family ledger recording the work and debts of sharecroppers on a cotton plantation in Carroll County, Mississippi : manuscript.
creator: LeFlore (Family : LeFlore, Greenwood, 1800-1865), creator.$$QLeFlore (Family
desc: Ledger recording the work and debts of primarily African-American sharecroppers and contract laborers on a cotton plantation in Carroll County, Mississippi owned by the LeFlore family, a prominent Choctaw family. The ledger contains entries for 50-60 men and women primarily for the years 1867-1869, but it also includes notes on corn and cotton production and accounts up to 1879. For each month of the 1867 and 1868 picking season, the ledger records the number of bales of cotton picked by each sharecropper. Beginning in 1869, a page is devoted to each of 60 "hands" (at least several of whom were likely former slaves belonging to the LeFlore family), which records his or her purchases of food, clothing, and supplies; debt to the plantation; credit from "cotton money"; and the balance due to the plantation. Other pages note livestock sold to sharecroppers and tools distributed to the heads of work squads. Notably, the ledger records no figures for interest due, suggesting that the sharecroppers were able to negotiate better terms than some of their peers in the Reconstruction-era South or that the LeFlore family did not engage in the practice of charging interest.

desc: This unique reference work provides students and the general public alike with coverage of more than 2,300 North American religious groups in the U.S. and Canada -- from Adventists to Zen Buddhists. The culmination of more than forty years of research, the information is presented in 26 chapters, each of which focuses on a different religious family. Each chapter includes an overview of the family's history, followed by directory entries on specific groups within that family. The directory entries provide factual information including, when available, rubrics for membership figures, educational facilities, and periodicals. This ninth edition of Melton's Encyclopedia of American Religions is an enormous leap forward for a title already acclaimed for its unique coverage. This edition is now two volumes instead of one, reflecting the expanded coverage of Canadian religion. Volume 1 covers the U.S., and Volume 2 covers Canada; both volumes include the same chapters for easy comparison between U.S. and Canadian religious expression. The Canadian volume also includes the Defunct Appendix (for all the religious groups that no longer exist), an alphabetical listing of all religious groups, a geographic listing for an additional way to search the content, and a subject index.-- Provided by publisher.

title: Divers traités sur la rhétorique, l'éloquence, la poësie, e l'histoire [17--]
creator: Gymnasium Immaculatae Conceptionis Societatis Iesu (Paris, France), former owner.$$QGymnasium Immaculatae Conceptionis Societatis Iesu (Paris, France) | Librairie Jean Clavreuil, bookseller.$$QLibrairie Jean Clavreuil
desc: Unsigned notebook, probably compiled in France during the 18th century, containing lectures and texts on rhetoric, eloquence, and oratory. The first section, arranged in seven chapters, presents general explanations of rhetoric and eloquence. The author compares the orator to the poet, the historian, and the philosopher, and also describes the perfect orator of Cicero and Aristotle. Other topics in this section deal with imitation, rhetorical figures, oratorical harmony, and invention.  The second section, entitled "Règles d'éloquence", develops the author's definitions and comparisons laid out in the first part, citing authorities such as La Fontaine, Racine, Livy, Horace, Euripides, Cicero, and Ovid. He also includes textual examples from classical Latin authors, such as Tacitus, Virgil, Livy, Horace, and from the Hexameron of St. Basil. The last section discusses rhetorical building blocks: the single sentence or thought ("pensée"); the "pensée" embellished as a "période" containing between 2 and 8 components; and the more complex "traité". Final sections discuss different kinds of descriptions: onomatopoetic (sound), topographical (place), chronographical (time/season), prosopographical (exterior appearance), and ethopoetic (character).

title: Manuscrit venu de Ste. Hèléne dune maniere inconnue [1817-1818].
creator: Lullin de Châteauvieux, Frédéric, 1772-1841.$$QLullin de Châteauvieux, Frédéric
desc: Ms. copy--transcribed from dictation by an anonymous copyist before 1820, probably between 1817 and 1818, and circulated clandestinely among Bonapartist circles--of a defense of Napoleon's character, motives, and actions, originally composed by the Genevan Jacob-Frédéric Lullin de Châteauvieux during the winter of 1816-1817. Lullin presents a favorable image of Napoleon as a solitary individual, observant, calculating, pragmatic--even impatient--whose behavior was motivated by self-interest.  The author praises Napoleon's love of military action, his loyalty to his men, his innate sense of strategy, and his overwhelming desire to serve the independence and grandeur of France. The Empire is naïvely portrayed as the heir to the Revolution of 1789, for its break with the Ancien régime, the Bourbons, the privileges of the aristocracy, and the tutelage of the Church, and Napoleon is seen as one who understood the key importance of the economy within the power structure, and who advocated strong political institutions and an efficient and centralized administration. Other prominent figures of the Empire mentioned by Lullin include Masséna, Dessaix, Ney, Bernadotte, Joséphine, and the Empress Marie-Louise of Augsburg.

title: 1872 Memoria general
creator: Philippines. Junta General de Estadística.$$QPhilippines. Junta General de Estadística.
desc: Annual report, issued by the Junta General de Estadística in Manila on Dec. 19, 1872, containing statistics on the geography, economy, education, and population of the Philippines for 1872. The report, prepared by the Junta in response to Real Orden No. 938 of Nov. 27, 1871, and signed by secretary Agustín de la Cavada, is divided into three sections: the first contains a brief history of the Junta and its commission; the second provides the statistical information collected by provincial officials and submitted to the Junta for tabulation; and the third describes the Junta's methodology in assembling the data, with suggestions for improving collection of information.  Included are geographical summaries by province; geographical locations; population statistics, classification of population by nationality, age, and religion; status of primary education, with number of schools and literacy levels; crime statistics; figures on housing construction, agricultural production by province, and imports and exports.  Bound with the report are copies, signed by Cavada, of the cover letter sent with the report by the Junta vice-president Brigadier Carlos Pavia to Rafael de Izquierdo, governor of the Philippines; and Izquierdo's reply to Pavia, acknowledging receipt of the report, and stating his intention to forward it to the Ministro de Ultramar for review.
